sections.heading: Why logic matters
sections.body: Programming specifications, database filters, and mathematical claims all depend on being clear about when a statement is true. Logic gives us a compact language for checking that clarity before an error turns into code.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.body: A proposition is a declarative sentence that is either true or false, but not both. For propositions p and q: ¬p means ‘not p’; p ∧ q is true only when both are true; p ∨ q is true when at least one is true; p → q is false only when p is true and q is false; p ↔ q is true when p and q have the same truth value.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Let p be ‘The server is online’ and q be ‘The database is reachable.’ The proposition p ∧ q means ‘The server is online and the database is reachable.’ It is true only if both component statements are true. In contrast, p → q says that being online is sufficient for being reachable; that claim is false only in the case p is true while q is false.

sections.heading: Common mistake
sections.body: In inclusive mathematical logic, ∨ includes the case where both p and q are true. If you need exactly one, write (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q).

sections.heading: Try it
sections.body: Let p be false and q be true. What is the truth value of ¬p ∧ q?
sections.tryAnswer: True. Since p is false, ¬p is true; both sides of the conjunction are true.

sections.heading: Why truth tables matter
sections.body: A truth table checks every possible assignment of truth values. That exhaustive view is valuable when you simplify a condition or prove that two expressions always agree.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.body: A truth table lists all truth assignments for the atomic propositions in an expression and evaluates the expression in each row. Two expressions are logically equivalent when they have the same truth value in every row. We write p ≡ q for logical equivalence.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Verify De Morgan’s law ¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q. If p and q are both true, both expressions are false. If either is false, p ∧ q is false, so its negation is true; at least one of ¬p or ¬q is also true. The same agreement holds in all four rows.

sections.heading: Common mistake
sections.body: An implication p → q is not the same as q → p. For example, ‘being a square implies being a rectangle’ is true, while the converse is not always true.

sections.heading: Try it
sections.body: Is p → q logically equivalent to ¬p ∨ q? Consider the one row where p is true and q is false, then the remaining rows.
sections.tryAnswer: Yes. Both expressions are false exactly when p is true and q is false, and true in the other three rows. This is a standard implication equivalence.

sections.heading: Why predicates matter
sections.body: A proposition has a settled truth value. A predicate becomes a proposition only after we specify an input or quantify over a domain. This is how discrete mathematics states rules about entire collections, not just one case.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.body: A predicate P(x) is a statement involving a variable x. The universal quantifier ∀x P(x) says P is true for every x in the chosen domain. The existential quantifier ∃x P(x) says there is at least one x in the domain for which P is true. The domain must always be understood or stated.
sections.diagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 620 200' role='img' aria-label='Set diagram showing universal and existential quantifiers'><circle cx='205' cy='105' r='72' fill='#eaf0ff' stroke='#04113A' stroke-width='3'/><circle cx='415' cy='105' r='72' fill='#edfff4' stroke='#01A54E' stroke-width='3'/><text x='205' y='47' text-anchor='middle' font-size='20' fill='#04113A'>∀: every member</text><text x='415' y='47' text-anchor='middle' font-size='20' fill='#04113A'>∃: at least one</text><g fill='#04113A'><circle cx='170' cy='93' r='8'/><circle cx='220' cy='120' r='8'/><circle cx='235' cy='80' r='8'/></g><circle cx='415' cy='105' r='11' fill='#FDEF03' stroke='#04113A' stroke-width='3'/><text x='205' y='190' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16' fill='#04113A'>all satisfy P(x)</text><text x='415' y='190' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16' fill='#04113A'>one witness satisfies P(x)</text></svg>

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Over the integers, let E(x) mean ‘x is even.’ The statement ∃x E(x) is true because 2 is a witness. The statement ∀x E(x) is false because 1 is a counterexample. Notice how one witness establishes an existential claim, while one counterexample refutes a universal claim.

sections.heading: Common mistake
sections.body: Negating a quantifier changes it: ¬∀x P(x) is equivalent to ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) is equivalent to ∀x ¬P(x). Do not merely place ¬ in front without changing the quantifier.

sections.heading: Try it
sections.body: Over the natural numbers, decide whether ∀n ∃m (m > n) is true.
sections.tryAnswer: True. For each natural number n, choose m = n + 1. This demonstrates that a different witness may be used for each n.
